Flash remediation — Phase 2b: the radial case

The Phase 2 radial (detector-channel truncation) story: geometry, the padding-scale sweeps across overshoots and regimes, and the channel-taper control · started 2026-07-08 · overview and other pages: index.html · the axial case: phase_2a_axial_results.html · plan of record: flash_remediation_plan.md · scripts: plans/experiments/flash_remediation/

TL;DR. For radial (channel) truncation, the answer is: pad the support to cover the object — no more, no less — and skip the channel taper. Throughout this page, overshoot means how far the object extends past the field of view: the ratio of the object's radius to the FoV radius, so overshoot 1.25× is an object 25% wider than the FoV. The padding knee sits at "cover" at every overshoot tested (1.1× to 4×) and in every regime (wide fan, sharp regularization, photon noise): every knee curve is a V with its minimum at — or, at larger overshoot, modestly beyond — cover, and the penalty is asymmetric (under-padding costs orders of magnitude, over-padding costs percent), so round the padding up when the object's extent is uncertain. The taper-only control confirmed the mechanism prediction exactly — it polishes the rim but leaves the interior bias untouched. Since "cover" depends on the object, the shipping policy needs a data-adaptive overshoot estimate (Phase 4). At extreme truncation, padding recovers structure but a smooth DC ambiguity remains — an information limit, not a remediation failure.

1  The geometry that frames the radial case

Notation (as in the axial page): SID — source-to-iso (rotation axis) distance; SDD — source-to-detector distance; C, δc — detector channel count and pitch; R — the field-of-view radius at the axis, R = (C/2)·δc·SID/SDD; overshoot — the object's radius as a multiple of R (an overshoot of 1.25× means the object's radius is 25% beyond the FoV; padding at scale s enlarges the support radius to s·R, so "cover" means scale ≈ overshoot). All lengths in the model's physical (ALU) units.

The axial page's central gift was a visibility bound: material beyond hmax·(SID+R)/SDD in z never projects, so full z-padding is always cheap. The radial case has no such bound. A point at any lateral distance from the axis is measured in some views — whenever the rotation brings it near the source–axis line, its ray passes close to the detector center, comfortably inside the fan. So arbitrarily distant material contaminates the sinogram, full padding must grow with the object, and the cost of covering it grows like the padded area. What bounds the problem instead is mechanics, not visibility: the object has to rotate in the gap between source and detector, so its radius cannot exceed min(SID, SDD−SID). That caps the worst-case padding scale at min(SID, SDD−SID)/R — a real ceiling (8× the FoV radius in our base geometry), but one set by clearances rather than by rays, and far above the scales real scans need. The two cartoons unpack both facts.

No lateral visibility bound — top view

Any material is measured in some views. The point P sits far outside the FoV, yet in the view drawn its ray (dashed red) runs down the source–axis line and lands mid-detector. As the gantry rotates, every point — however far out — passes through such views, so there is no radial analog of the axial visibility bound: distant material always contaminates part of the sinogram, and only enlarging the support can explain it.

The physical rotation bound — top view

Mechanics set the only hard stop. The rotating object sweeps a cylinder that must fit between the source and the detector: Robj < min(SID, SDD−SID). The worst-case padding scale is therefore min(SID, SDD−SID)/R — 8× the FoV radius in our base geometry (SID = SDD/2). Everything between the FoV and that circle is fair game for a real object, which is why the padding policy must track the object's actual overshoot rather than quote one geometric number.

2  Experiment design

All variants reuse the Phase 1 lateral setup (cone beam, magnification 2, 128 views, thin 32-slice slab, cylinder phantom with three embedded spheres, contained in z) and are judged as before: ring/interior NRMSE against the ground truth phantom, montages with the metric region outlined, radial profiles, and convergence on recon − ground truth. Four groups of variants:

  • Core padding-scale sweep (overshoot 1.25×, default regularization, no noise): scales {1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.35 ≈ cover, 1.5 over-cover control}, plus the channel-taper-only falsification control and a pad + taper combo.
  • Overshoot axis: scale sets at overshoots 1.1× and 1.5× that bracket each object's own cover and continue until the curve turns ({1.0, 1.05, 1.12, 1.2, 1.35} and {1.0, 1.25, 1.45, 1.6, 1.85, 2.1, 2.4, 2.8}), so every curve can show the descent, the minimum, and the reversal beyond it — is "cover the object" always the knee, and what does partial padding buy?
  • Extreme overshoot showcase (4× the FoV — half the physical rotation bound): {1.0, 2.5, 4.1 ≈ cover, 4.6} — the stress test the axial case could not have, since only mechanics bounds the radial problem.
  • Regime riders, each an independent single-variable probe at scales {1.0, 1.2, 1.35 ≈ cover, 1.5}: wide fan (SID and SDD shortened together at fixed magnification, R/SID 0.125→0.2), sharp regularization (sharpness 2 / snr_db 35, run to 160 iterations per the axial convergence lesson), and photon noise + transmission weights at default regularization.

The key summary figure will be the knee curves — ring and interior NRMSE versus padding scale, one curve per overshoot and per regime — which directly answer whether the knee moves and what the policy should be.

3  Results

Every variant reported below is converged — change-% at the final iteration is at most 0.1, and the region metrics are flat over the last twenty iterations — so the two surprises below are properties of the converged solutions, not transients. One incidental validation before any reconstruction ran: the rotation-bound check from §1 rejected the first wide-fan configuration outright, because shrinking only SDD left the 1.25× object exactly touching the detector — the physical bound is not hypothetical. (The fix: shorten SID and SDD together at fixed magnification.)

The core sweep: the knee is at "cover the object"

Two details worth pausing on. First, over-cover padding mildly hurts here (1.5's 0.099/0.100 vs cover's 0.063/0.081), and it is converged — a genuine contrast with the axial case, where padding past the visibility bound changed nothing at all. The mechanism difference is exactly the §1 geometry: axial beyond-bound voxels receive no rays, while extra lateral voxels intersect real rays and participate — which also means the beyond-cover behavior is object-dependent rather than an exact tie (the knee curves below show the V's minimum shifting modestly past cover at larger overshoot, though the beyond-minimum penalty stays shallow everywhere). Second, the pad + taper combo buys a small ring improvement at partial padding (0.207 → 0.189, interior unchanged) — unlike the axial case where tapering always hurt — but it is nowhere near competitive with just padding to cover.

What this settles

The radial recommendation: pad the support to cover the object, with a modest margin — rounding up when uncertain — and skip the channel taper entirely. Every knee curve is a V whose minimum sits at cover (small overshoot) or modestly beyond it (larger overshoot); under-padding is the steep side of the V, costing orders of magnitude, while over-padding costs percent plus ~scale² memory. The taper is now doubly retired (it cannot reach the interior bias here, just as it starved end slices in the axial case). Because there is no geometric formula for "cover" — the object's extent is not knowable from the scanner geometry — the shipping policy needs an estimate of the object's overshoot, which is exactly the data-adaptive truncation detector sketched in the plan (edge-channel level above the air floor); that design moves to Phase 4. For severely truncated scans, set expectations by the extreme showcase: padding recovers structure, while absolute values may carry an unresolvable smooth offset.

4  Reproduction

Script: plans/experiments/flash_remediation/radial_pad_sweep.py (shared machinery in truncation_common.py; the variant groups are selectable at the top of the file, so subsets can run independently). Runs on CPU or GPU. Figures land in figures/p2b_* and are embedded here via embed_report_figures.py; metrics and final volumes in results/p2b_*.
